questions.explanation: The five tests are not equally hard, and the reason is that a forger can buy or borrow the first three and cannot invent the fifth. Material requires a skin of the right kind, and a forger with a blank of the right period has one. Writing requires a competent hand, and a competent hand can be acquired or copied from a specimen. The seal is harder, but a forger in possession of a genuine seal can impress it, and wax and parchment can be matched. The wording can be copied too. What cannot be matched is the company the document keeps: a charter must name a person in office, an event, a boundary, a boundary-stone, a place-name, and a set of formulae, all at the date alleged. The conjunction has to be possible, and that is why the fifth test is the one that convicts. The traps each name a test as decisive on a ground the extract contradicts. Neither material nor a seal is beyond imitation, and a hand can be imitated well enough to need a comparison at all.

stimulus.body: From a manual of the method of examining old charters, in a late seventeenth-century compilation of the rules. The question is to be asked in five ways. First, of the material: of what the skin is made, and whether it is of the kind used in that country at the time alleged. Secondly, of the writing: whether the hand agrees with other instruments of that date and place, and whether the letters are formed as they were formed in that office in that time. Thirdly, of the seal: whether the wax is of the age of the skin, and whether the impression answers to the seal of the person named in the grant. Fourthly, of the wording: whether the titles, the address and the formulae are such as were used in that office in that century, and whether the benefit granted is one that office could grant. Fifthly, of the company the document keeps: whether it names a ruler holding office, a frontier, a river, a boundary-stone, a place or a person, and whether each of the things it names is attested elsewhere at that time, and whether they were all of them possible at once.

questions.explanation: A dated exemplar supplies a fixed point, and that is the whole difference. Agreement with it says two things at once: that the two instruments came from the same office, and that the practice of the hand and the seal was already in use at a known date. An undated exemplar establishes only the first, and the same practice may have been in use for a century and a half, so agreement with it places the document somewhere in a long interval rather than at a date. That is a real difference in what the test can conclude, not a difference in how carefully it is done. The traps each confuse the two things the comparison establishes. Certainty does not transfer from a dated instrument to an undated one by association; what transfers is a range, not a point. A date is not a script, so legibility is a separate matter. And the test is not about which office made a document, which agreement already shows, but about when a way of writing and sealing was in use, which is what makes a date possible at all.

questions.explanation: A printed transcript stands at one remove from the document, and the remove is unrecorded. A fourteenth-century copy may have been made from the charter or from an earlier copy, and the printed text cannot distinguish the two, because it reproduces the copy and not the charter. So the authority the reasoning borrows is the authority of a witness of unknown date, and it is being used to certify a document of a different date. The test for this is the second of the five: a transcript of unknown date is of no help in dating anything. The traps each get the relation wrong. Age is a ground of confidence and not of distrust, and a later transcript can be a faithful witness to an older text. Editorial choice is a real problem for printed texts, but it is not the only one and not the one that makes the certificate circular. And the last option reverses the dependency: a charter is evidence of what an office did, and a later belief about a charter is evidence about the later belief.

The document that survives was not made in the ninth century, whatever it says; and yet a copy made two or three centuries later can carry a text whose substance is older, because the practice of copying an earlier grant into a new instrument is ordinary. So a later hand establishes a terminus for the surviving object and does not by itself fix the date of the transaction recorded in it. This is the ordinary situation in the subject, and the whole practice of testing exists to manage it. The traps each take the finding further than it goes. questions.explanation: The incentive and the survival of the document are the same fact seen from two sides. A grant is worth nothing in a dispute unless the house can produce the instrument, and a produced instrument is a piece of paper in a box that can be produced again. So a house with a weak claim has the most to gain from a strong-looking paper and the most to lose by losing one, and the same house is the one in whose archive the paper is most likely to be found, because a forger has no reason to deposit it anywhere else. That is the ordinary asymmetry of forgery: it leaves its traces where its beneficiary is. The traps each add a detail the mechanism does not require. Payment was normally a single sum, not a piece rate, so there was no output incentive. And an incentive is not a description of how often forgery actually occurred. A forger working from a genuine seal could indeed be meticulous, but that is a matter of craft, not of motive, and it is not the explanation of why the documents survive where they do.

questions.explanation: The clause does something procedural rather than administrative, and that is why it has lasted. A rule that all archives form one body and are under one authority means that a series of deposits can be planned: the arrangement can be designed while the papers are still in the churches and the offices, so that a deposit arriving in 1796 can be put where it belongs instead of being made to fit what has already been shelved. questions.explanation: The categories are the evidence. A class for deeds and accounts and a class for charters and manuscripts is a division by what a document is evidence of, not by when it was made and not by who received it. The person who made that division was therefore reading the suppressed church's papers as a set of administrative acts, and expecting to be able to ask questions of them later about rights, revenues and jurisdictions. That is the beginning of history as it is now practised, and it is not a judgement about the value of the papers: an inventory of a granary is not less historical than a chronicle. The traps each misdescribe the division. The officials were not indifferent to the church's history, and the larger class was kept precisely because it could be used. The division is not chronological, which is the commonest arrangement and would have cut across the deposits. And a class is not small because its contents are uninteresting; a class of charters and manuscripts is comparatively small because most of what a large institution writes is a receipt.

questions.explanation: The order is the substantive claim of the arrangement, and it is a claim about where meaning lives. A paper's sense very often depends on the company it kept: a register is intelligible as the record of one office's procedure and is close to unintelligible if its entries are distributed among boxes labelled by subject, since the sequence, the numbering and the cross-references are all part of what the entries mean. So the arrangement goes from the producer, where the meaning is guaranteed, to the subject, where the usefulness is. The rule of not breaking a deposit follows directly, and it has a cost that has been argued over ever since: a question that cuts across offices has to be answered from several series. The traps each explain the rule by something other than meaning. Cost is a reason to prefer a plan, not a reason for a methodological rule. Abolition of offices did not silence the paper trail. And nothing about an arrangement of deposits carries a legal bar against combining them.

questions.explanation: A deposit is held together by its producer, not by its place, its date, or its kind of act. questions.explanation: The construction is the oldest case in the subject and it is a model of the reasoning the test exists to break. A document is dated to an age that would support one claim; the date is then used to support a second; and the second claim, resting on the date, is used to confirm the first. Two claims are being supported by one piece of evidence and each is being offered as evidence for the other, so the support is entirely circular and the document has been asked to confirm itself. The test that dissolves this is the fifth of the five, because a false date makes the company the document keeps impossible: the people, places and events it names cannot all be where it says they are. A claim long maintained is not a claim well founded. stimulus.body: From a letter of invitation sent out in 1819, printed with the list of those who had answered it. It is proposed that the undersigned should form themselves into a society for the study of older German history, whose object shall be the production of a complete edition of the writers who are the sources of German history in the Middle Ages. The undertaking is to be begun with private means and by subscription, and each subscriber will be asked to contribute according to his means and will receive the volumes as they appear, his name being printed in the first volume. The society will hold no meetings and will keep no premises. The work is to be carried on by correspondence among its members, and the direction of the edition will rest with a central board. It is not proposed that the society should take up any question of opinion; and nothing will be published which is not a text, together with such apparatus as the editor is able to give it.

questions.explanation: The list is a definition, and it is worth noticing how quietly it makes one. A history of Germany, on this plan, consists of written acts and records: a law is enacted, a charter is granted, a letter is written, a chronicle is kept. Anything that was not written is not a source for this history but an object for another kind of enquiry. That is a large commitment and it shaped what the resulting series could be used for, decades after the plan was written. The traps each misread the list as provisional, as a priority order, or as an oversight. A list that says what is to be produced is a definition of the subject, and it is not a shopping list to be enlarged. Laws are one item among four and not the frame for the other three. And the exclusion of the unwritten record is not a failure of imagination; it is a consequence of having defined the subject as a body of texts, which is the ordinary condition of a subject that begins by editing.

stimulus.body: From a lecture given to the pupils of a school of charters in the later nineteenth century. Every one of you will find things in the arrangement of these depots which you would do otherwise, and I do not blame you for it. A better system is always to be had, I am told, and the man who has one may be recommended to do as he pleases. But we make very little progress in pursuing perfection, which is unattainable, while our changes, each of them reasonable in itself, are a constant source of irremediable loss of time. Imperfect as our organisation is, it is an accomplished fact. In matters of this kind it is the first thing necessary, next to the usefulness of the thing itself, that it should be fixed. A reference given in one year ought to be findable in another, and a paper described in a catalogue ought to be on the shelf where the catalogue says it is. Let no one take this for a counsel of sloth. It is the condition of all work of this kind, and the first thing a beginner has to learn is that he is not the person who pays for the tidying up.

The corpus is an accumulation: every stone that can be read has to be found, seen, copied and described, and the work is done by a network of contributors in a dozen countries, so the institution that is doing it is not the institution that is doing the seeing. That is the reason such undertakings are attached to academies rather than to scholars, and it is why a decade is a normal interval and not a sign of difficulty. A student who expects a project's scale to be visible in one career will misread every one of these. The traps each supply a different explanation for the interval. A decision that precedes the work by ten years is not a decision taken in a hurry, and the inscriptions had indeed been described piecemeal for centuries without being gathered. And the interval is not a period of training, since contributors were qualified long before the authorisation.

questions.explanation: A printed text is an account of a stone, and the difference matters here more than anywhere else in the discipline. The letters on a stone are damaged in ways a copy smooths over: an erasure, a letter cut over another, a line lost at a break, a surface worn on one side and not the other. So a printed text cannot show what kind of object it was taken from, and the alternatives can only be judged by somebody who has seen the object and can say which reading suits it. Requiring the stone in person converts an edition of inscriptions into a record of the inscriptions, and the drawing, the squeeze and the setting are what allow the judgement to be repeated by somebody who never travels. The traps each give a different reason for the requirement. Travel is not the aim of the work. Cost does not generate a rule about verification. And a manuscript can be sent by post just as easily as a stone can be carried, so difficulty of access is not the explanation either.

questions.explanation: An interval between two dates is the difference between them, not the number of years you land on while counting. From 1853 to 1863 is 1863 minus 1853, which is ten years, and that is the figure the institution's own history of the corpus gives when it says the first volume appeared ten years after the financing was approved. questions.explanation: A history of Rome in three volumes, followed by a second edition and then by a corpus of the sources, is a programme and not a book. The sequence says that the argument could not be trusted unless the reader could check it, which is why the sources came after the conclusions rather than with them. And the fact that the book was read as an answer to a named school abroad says that the dispute shaped what the evidence was held to show: when two schools disagree about the character of a state, the same inscriptions and the same histories can be read in opposite ways, and the reading is the argument. The traps each deny one of those three features. The author had the rival scholarship in front of him, and the whole dispute is about what it means. The work was not a translation. And the collected sources were published, which is the opposite of a withholding, though a second edition produced within a few years is a good indication of how unsettled the ground was.

questions.explanation: The distinguishing feature of a seminar is that the claims are the students' and the criticism is the other students'. That makes it the only efficient way to teach the parts of the craft that are not rules: how much a document will bear, how far a comparison can be pushed, when a coincidence is a coincidence, how to be wrong in public without abandoning the work. A course of lectures can convey the narrative and the arguments; it cannot convey those judgements, because they are exercised rather than stated. And a seminar works only if the students have access to the documents, which is why the two are inseparable. The traps each substitute a different object of instruction. Content can be got from a book. A teacher's opinions are the one thing a seminar exists to prevent being merely received. And knowing where the documents are can be learnt, and was learnt in the library, but it is not what a seminar is for.

questions.explanation: A rule of citation is a rule about checkability, and checkability requires two things that are not the same. It requires the method, which is the habit of stating a reference, and it requires access, which is a deposit that is open, described and found. A method without access is a style; an access without a method is a room full of boxes. So the history of the discipline and the history of its repositories are one history, and the opening and describing of a great collection belongs in it as squarely as the invention of a way of reading. The traps each misdescribe what the habit is. It is not an economy of space. And a citation is the opposite of a confession of mistrust, since a document is being produced so that it can be checked. Nor is it the property of one institution; it is a convention that travels with a generation and is still in use.

questions.explanation: The claim is a separation, and the two halves of it are the separation and the consequence. The study of the past has a method that can be described and taught, and using it well is incompatible with a stake in the verdict, because a stake operates on the weighing of evidence and not only on the conclusion. Notice what is not being said. It is not said that political history is not a subject; the most politically committed writing of the period came out of this very generation. It is not said that a historian must hold no opinions, since the man who holds none has no reason to weigh anything. And it is not a claim that one science outranks another, since the argument is about what makes a particular kind of enquiry reliable, not about which enquiry is higher. The traps each inflate the claim into an exclusion it never makes.

questions.explanation: Fifty-six years of voluntary work, ending in a reconstitution with a seat and public money, is a fact about scale. A series of this kind outlasts any one group of subscribers, and a generation of scholars who found themselves responsible for a volume tend to find that they are paying for it out of their own money, which is not a sustainable arrangement for a project intended to be complete. So the passage from private subscription to a public institution is not a verdict on the original plan, which was correct about the need and impossible about the means. It is the point at which the plan and the means were separated. The traps each misread the interval. A difficulty of funding is not a proof that the plan was mistaken. Nor is it evidence that the subscribers lost interest, since the work continued throughout. And a reconstitution in 1875 is not a finishing date: a series of medieval sources is still being edited today, and the volumes of 1875 were the beginning of a long second phase rather than the end of the first.

questions.explanation: Three of the four follow from the arrangement. And an obligation on offices to deposit their papers makes the deposit a by-product of administration, so the supply is regular instead of being a matter of what a retiring clerk decides to send. No archive, state or otherwise, has a power to settle a conclusion, and a discipline that depended on such a power would have stopped being a discipline the moment the institution changed its mind.

questions.explanation: The practical business was the point, and it was practical in a specific sense: the work exceeded what one archive or one country could do, so the only way to make progress was to divide it and to fix the division before anybody began. A list of the documents to be printed is a promise that two scholars will not both edit the same text and that neither will leave it alone; a plan for a catalogue is a promise that the description of a manuscript will mean the same thing in two countries. Both are things that cannot be secured by correspondence, because the difficulty is precisely that the parties did not know what the other was doing. The traps each misdescribe what a congress is. questions.explanation: The view draws a distinction that a good deal of later work turned on, namely between the age of a document and the age of the things it records. On this view a late document saying that such and such was done in the fourth century is evidence for the late document and for the belief of its compiler, and only indirectly for the fourth century, and the indirectness has to be argued rather than assumed. That is a sound methodological position, and it cost the eighteenth century a great deal, because it threw out a large body of material on a point that later work handled by collation and by internal criticism rather than by rejection. The traps each go beyond the view. A view about how a document is to be read is not an argument for destroying the document. And the view does not say that the early period is inaccessible, only that particular documents do not give direct access to it. Nothing in it concerns the reputation of the body that produced the document.

questions.explanation: The two lists answer two different questions, and the different arrangements follow from the questions. A list of a man's own writings arranged by year is a chronology of his work, and its use is to see the order in which his positions were taken up and abandoned; a list of the works he used arranged by publisher is a finding aid, and its use is to send a reader to the place where a thing may be read, which is not the same as the place where it was written. stimulus.body: Notice issued by a learned society in the eighteenth century, asking for materials for a survey of a province. The society is engaged in a description of the parishes, the roads, the soils, the manufactures and the antiquities of the province, and it desires that those who hold papers should send them. It is not proposed to print the papers themselves; they are to be used in the preparation of descriptions, and the society will return them to the sender within the year. Where a document cannot be spared, a copy will be made at the society's charge. Persons who possess a copy of an old register, a map, a rental, a Terrier or a local history, and who know no more of it than that it is old, are asked to give notice of it, though they may be wholly unable to read it. The society does not desire narratives. It will pay for no information which cannot be brought to a document.

questions.explanation: The two arrangements are not a better and a worse version of the same thing; they buy different things, and the price of each is the other. Arranging by the producer guarantees that a paper is never separated from the company that gives it meaning, and the price is that a question crossing offices has to be answered from several series. Arranging by subject makes a cross-cutting question a single journey through the shelves, and the price is that the sequence and the cross-references within a series, which are part of the meaning, are broken. That is why the choice has been argued over for two centuries and why most arrangements now do a little of each, keeping whole deposits together and providing subject guides across them. The traps each collapse the trade-off. The difference is one of principle and not of date. Grouping by subject does not destroy the evidence of sequence, because a folder of a single subject is usually a folder of one office's acts about that subject. And the choice is not settled by what the work costs.

questions.explanation: A title that names a field is a statement about what the journal will print, and it is made before any of the work exists. It is therefore a commitment rather than a description, and it has effects in both directions. It gives contributors a subject to write for, which is what a new school needs; and it makes the journal unusable for anything outside the field, which is a real cost and one the founders accepted. The opposite choice, a title that named nothing, would have avoided the commitment and would have left the journal without a constituency. The traps each read the title as something other than a programme. A title is not a diplomatic courtesy, since naming the field is the surest way of announcing a position. Nothing suggests an earlier plan for a society. And a title is not a promissory note: the subject existed, it was growing, and what was new was the intention to be the place where it was published.

A chronicler writing about a town in the nineteenth century has sources, and the phrases he finds in them are phrases those sources used. questions.explanation: The order is fixed by length, and that is the whole argument of the scheme, since what distinguishes the three is the rate of change and not the subject. The slowest is the time of the land and of the habits built on it, which is why it is described as almost immobile and why a lifetime does not witness any of it. The middle is the time of the movements a generation can see moving: a curve of prices, a run of good or bad harvests, a population rising and falling. questions.explanation: The register has the one thing a chronicle does not, which is completeness in a defined column. A chronicle records what its writer thought worth writing, and the omissions are a judgement; a register has a column for the dead and the column is filled, so a parish can be counted for a year rather than estimated. questions.explanation: Three of the four are uses the series can bear. A price series shows the direction and the size of a movement in that price over a period longer than any memory, which is the whole point of a series. Set against a wage series from the same places and years it gives the purchasing power of a wage, which is a real wage and not a money wage, and that comparison is the only way the number becomes an argument about how people lived. And an erratic movement out of all proportion to the general run points to a failed harvest, which is a causal claim a series can carry when the other movements are regular. The excluded option is the one the series cannot do. questions.explanation: The two documents are evidence for two different things and for neither of the thing an investigator most wants. The petition is evidence that the men in those households wanted a change, and evidence of something more interesting, namely that they were able to put it in writing, sign it together and get it delivered. The entry in the minute book is evidence of what the authority was willing to write down and to do, and of the vocabulary in which a government refused. Neither records what followed, and a reader who supplies the outcome from general knowledge is adding something to the record that neither document contains. The traps each make one of the documents carry more than it can. Both entries are contemporary, so the difference is not one of date. Neither is more reliable than the other in general, since their reliability is exactly what each is good for. questions.explanation: The consequence is that a deposit has a history of its own, and that history is a filter standing between the past and the reader. A transfer can drop what the receiving office had no use for; a gift comes with the judgement of the giver; a fire or a lost wagon removes whatever was in the room; a seizure removes whatever the seizing power had no interest in. So the absence of a document from an archive is evidence, at best, about the archive and not about the past, and the two have to be told apart before any inference is drawn from a silence. This is the single largest difference between a modern deposit and the record of an office that kept its own papers. The traps each make the opposite assumption. Transfers are not lossless. A finding aid is not a chronology, since papers are arranged by the office that received them and not by when things happened. And a question asked and not answered is a different state of knowledge from a question not yet asked, and the difference is worth recording.

questions.explanation: The reference is the instrument's account of itself. It says that the ordinance is made in the form a power already claimed allows, and it therefore presents the school not as a new thing but as the exercise of a standing right. In the circumstances that is not decoration. The kingdom had been through a revolution, an abolition of the old bodies and a restoration, and a new school for reading old documents could be presented in more than one way: as a repair of something interrupted, which is what the preamble says, or as an innovation by a regime that had abolished most of what it was now reviving. The formula removes the second reading by putting the act inside a continuous claim. The traps each read the reference as something other than what it is. A formula of this kind is the opposite of a formality, since it is where the instrument states its authority. And a power to make regulations is not a subordination of the school to anything, so nothing here makes the school dissolvable. Nor is a citation of authority an attribution of authorship.

questions.explanation: The inference rests on simultaneity, and simultaneity is the weakest of the reasons available. Two things happening at once establishes that both were possible in the same period, which is a real finding, and it does not establish that either produced the other. There is a direction to be fixed and a magnitude to be measured, and both are missing. The point is not that the connection is implausible; ports and industry are connected often enough that a historian would take the pair seriously. The point is that the pair is not yet a cause, and a strong answer goes on to say what would make it one, which is a mechanism stated in terms of that region and that period, and evidence that the mechanism operated. The traps each supply a different defect. Nothing in the observation makes the connection absurd. A demand for a further cause is not a refusal of this one. And the years of the works are given, so the defect is not in the dating.
questions.hint: What does the coincidence of two events in the same decades establish about each of them?

answer.exemplar: First, the figure itself: was it counted or estimated, was it copied from a summary, or was it computed, and can I do the arithmetic again from the account? A reported total and a computed total fail differently, and that is where a transcription slip hides. Second, the series behind it: is the record complete for the years in question, and did the practice that generated the accounts change during the period, because a change in the practice moves the number with no change in the world at all. Third, the comparison that makes the figure striking: it is only remarkable against another figure, and the two have to be the same commodity, in the same money, over the same places, defined in the same way, or the strikingness is an artefact of how I compared them. And I would end by saying what the surviving figure does and does not show: it is evidence about the accounts that record it, and not a direct measurement of the thing being described, so an argument built on it has to carry that limit with it.

questions.explanation: The three questions are not three requests for more information of the same kind; they attack three different things, and a number is exposed to each separately. The first attacks the figure. Was it counted, estimated, copied from somebody's summary, or arrived at by arithmetic, and can the arithmetic be done again from the account itself? A reported total and a computed total fail in different ways, and the difference between them is where transcription slips live. The second attacks the series behind the figure. Is the record behind it complete, and did the practice that produced it change during the period, since a change in the practice produces a change in the number with no change in the world. The third attacks the comparison that makes the figure striking, because a figure is only remarkable against another, and the two must be the same commodity in the same money over the same places defined in the same way, or the strikingness is an artefact of the comparison rather than a fact about the past. An answer that also names the limit of its own conclusion is stronger still: a figure that survives all three questions is evidence about the accounts that record it, and not a direct measurement of the thing being described.
questions.hint: The figure, the series behind it, and the comparison it is remarkable against are three different things, and each can fail on its own.
